claims.text: Hormone therapy (estrogen, a progestogen, or both) is the most effective tx for menopausal symptoms
claims.quote: Hormone therapy (estrogen, a progestogen, or both) is the most effective treatment for menopausal symptoms (1).

claims.text: Conjugated estrogens + bazedoxifene (a SERM) is an option for women with a uterus, without a progestogen;
claims.quote: Bazedoxifene acts as an estrogen receptor antagonist in the endometrium and protects against endometrial cancer; thus, a progestogen is not needed.

claims.text: very-low-dose vaginal estrogen also needs no progestogen
claims.quote: the exception to this is very low dose vaginal estrogen therapy (used for genitourinary syndrome of menopause), which can be given without a progestogen. Another option for women with a uterus is the combination of conjugated estrogens with bazedoxifene.

claims.text: Start with the lowest dose;
claims.quote: Treatment should start with the lowest dose;

claims.text: low-dose transdermal hormone therapy may carry less risk of DVT and stroke
claims.quote: low-dose transdermal hormone therapy may have less risk of deep venous thrombosis and stroke.

claims.text: A progestogen alone (eg, medroxyprogesterone acetate) is sometimes used when estrogen is contraindicated, but is less effective for hot flushes and doesn't relieve vaginal dryness
claims.quote: Progestogens are sometimes used alone (eg, medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg orally once a day or depot 150 mg IM once a month, megestrol acetate 10 to 20 mg orally once a day, micronized progesterone 300 mg nightly) when estrogen is contraindicated, but they are not as effective as estrogen for hot flushes and do not relieve vaginal dryness.

claims.text: Nonhormonal options for hot flushes: neurokinin receptor antagonists, SSRIs (eg, paroxetine), SNRIs (eg, venlafaxine), gabapentin, oxybutynin;
claims.quote: Consider neurokinin receptor antagonists (eg, fezolinetant), elinzanetant (if available), SSRIs (eg, paroxetine salt), SNRIs (eg, venlafaxine), oxybutynin, or gabapentin as alternatives to MHT for relieving hot flushes.

claims.text: all are less effective than hormone therapy
claims.quote: however, all of these medications are less effective than hormone therapy

claims.text: Fezolinetant (selective neurokinin-3 receptor antagonist): for vasomotor symptoms;
claims.quote: Neurokinin receptor antagonists are indicated to treat menopausal vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes, night sweats); available medications in this class include fezolinetant, a selective neurokinin-3 receptor antagonist (10, 11, 12)

claims.text: AEs abdominal pain, diarrhea, insomnia, back pain, hot flushes, rare liver injury
claims.quote: For fezolinetant, potential side effects include abdominal pain, diarrhea, difficulty sleeping, back pain, hot flushes, and rare reports of liver injury.

claims.text: → check LFTs before starting;
claims.quote: Liver function tests are needed before starting fezolinetant

claims.text: contraindicated with CYP1A2 inhibitors (eg, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine)
claims.quote: Fezolinetant is contraindicated in patients using CYP1A2 inhibitors (eg, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, and other medications).

claims.text: Fezolinetant BOXED WARNING (FDA, Dec 2024): hepatotoxicity.
claims.quote: Boxed Warning, Hepatotoxicity 12/2024

claims.text: Check LFTs before starting,
claims.quote: Perform hepatic laboratory tests prior to initiation of treatment to evaluate for hepatic function and injury.

claims.text: monthly for the first 3 mo, then at 6 and 9 mo;
claims.quote: Perform follow-up hepatic laboratory testing monthly for the first 3 months, at 6 months, and 9 months of treatment (2.1, 5.1).

claims.text: stop if LFTs >5× ULN or >3× ULN with bilirubin >2× ULN
claims.quote: Discontinue VEOZAH if transaminase elevations are > 5 x ULN, or if transaminase elevations are > 3 x ULN and the total bilirubin level is > 2 x ULN.

claims.text: Elinzanetant (Lynkuet; dual NK1/NK3 receptor antagonist,
claims.quote: LYNKUET is a neurokinin 1 (NK1) and neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptor antagonist indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms due to menopause. (1)
Initial U.S. Approval: 2025

claims.text: another nonhormonal option for moderate–severe vasomotor symptoms;
claims.quote: LYNKUET is indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms (VMS) due to menopause.

claims.text: AEs headache, fatigue, somnolence
claims.quote: The most frequently reported (≥5%) adverse reactions were headache, fatigue, dizziness and somnolence. (6.1)

claims.text: Gabapentin 300 mg up to 3 times daily is effective and well tolerated; pregabalin is not recommended
claims.quote: Gabapentin (300 mg up to 3 times daily) has been shown to be effective and well-tolerated (14). However, pregabalin is not recommended due to limited efficacy data and risk of adverse effects, including potential substance misuse.

claims.text: Oxybutynin (anticholinergic used for overactive bladder) treats vasomotor symptoms: 2.5 or 5 mg twice daily, or up to 15 mg extended-release once daily
claims.quote: Oxybutynin, an anticholinergic that is used to treat overactive bladder, also effectively treats vasomotor symptoms (doses in studies have included 2.5 or 5 mg twice daily; or up to 15 mg extended-release once daily) (13).

claims.text: Clonidine is not recommended: it is less effective than the other nonhormonal options
claims.quote: Other nonhormonal medications that are not recommended are suvorexant (a dual orexin-receptor antagonist), due to limited efficacy data, and clonidine, because it is less effective than other nonhormonal treatment options (1).
